newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine "Public Enemy" says he's just a postman.
newsitem.headline: Argentine "Public Enemy" says he's just a postman.

text.p: A businessman said by ex-Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo to be Argentina's godfather of organised crime was accused by a congressional committee on Thursday of building a "state within the state."

But in a 6-1/2-hour grilling by a security commitee of both houses, postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran said he was "just a postman" who had become the "most maligned man in Argentina" since Cavallo began his anti-mafia campaign in mid-1995.

Congress had summoned Yabran to clarify his interests in private security firms allegedly linked to the recent murder of a news photographer. But the committee questioned him on all aspects of reports of murky dealings that have portrayed him to be, as he called it, Argentina's "Public Enemy No.1."

The tall, silver-haired, blue-eyed businessman has acknowledged he has assets of $400 million and is said to be a friend of President Carlos Menem. The Peronist president denies it, but his ex-wife insists the two are friends.

Yabran is suing Cavallo, whose free-market policies earned him world renown before he was fired last year, for accusing him of building a big stake in postal and airport businesses for criminal ends. Cavallo has named government ministers and judges whom he said helped Yabran.
Congress has taken up Cavallo's crusade and plans to set up a special anti-mafia committee this week whose first task will be to investigate Yabran.

While Yabran told the committee he was just "the postman of a big economic group," deputies like Carlos Alvarez, head of the opposition Frepaso alliance, accused him of building up "power in the shadows in sensitive and strategic areas" and of "constructing almost a state within the state."

The Yabran case has stretched from Catholic clergymen in the city of Cordoba, who took his money in donations, to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, whose firm did some consultancy work for Yabran.

The formerly secretive tycoon's spokesman, Wenceslao Bunge, said Yabran had been "forced into the public spotlight by the horrendous murder" of news photographer Jose Luis Cabezas in January. News reports linked security firms allegedly owned by Yabran with the Noticias magazine photographer's killing.
Cabezas, who worked on stories about police corruption and about Yabran, was handcuffed and shot and his body burned.

Yabran denies ownership of security firms or any link with the crime. He took out a full-page ad in the Argentine press on Thursday accusing Cavallo of trying "to make me Public Enemy No. 1" with politically motivated "hysterical verbiage."
